name: Clustering Illusion
description: People see meaningful streaks, hot spots, or clusters in random noise because ordinary lumpiness feels too patterned to be chance. Randomness often looks less evenly mixed than intuition expects.
design_relevance_note: Relevant when teams interpret heatmaps, bug bursts, complaint spikes, fraud events, or analytics anomalies: a short run of nearby events can look like a deep pattern before anyone checks whether random variation could generate the same shape.
myth_risk_note: The textbook claim that belief in performance "streaks" is purely a cognitive illusion is a strong candidate for a scientific myth: Miller & Sanjurjo (2018, Econometrica) mathematically demonstrated a hidden selection-bias error in the foundational 1985 study, and correcting for it reveals a real, statistically significant hot-hand effect in the original data; independent MLB evidence (Green & Zwiebel 2017) corroborates real streak phenomena. This is a widely-cited textbook example that recent, methodologically rigorous work substantially overturns.
prevalence_note: Known in decision science, gambling/data-literacy, and analytics skepticism, but not a mainstream named heuristic in general design practice.

findings.description: The same law-of-small-numbers intuition led people to expect each short segment of a random sequence to mirror the overall proportion, making ordinary streaks and local clumps seem overly diagnostic and feeding gambler's-fallacy-style misperception of randomness.
findings.source_title: Belief in the law of small numbers.
